issues.legal_issue: A consent decree founded on a purported family arrangement is a nullity when the circumstances establish that the arrangement and the proceedings were fraudulent.
material_facts: The suit was filed, the written statement admitting the claim was filed, the defendant's statement was recorded, and the decree was passed within a few days.
The defendant was an illiterate woman who was brought to court on the stated pretext of executing a lease, and the evidence indicated that she trusted the plaintiff.

The plaint alleged that a family arrangement had transferred the defendant's entire share and possession to the plaintiff, but the defendant remained in possession and the revenue entries continued in her name.
The plaintiff had no apparent antecedent claim to the property, the defendant received nothing in return, and her daughter and son-in-law were excluded without an apparent reason.

The decree referred only to the defendant's consent in the written statement and did not address the alleged family arrangement; the defendant's thumb impression and statement were obtained in the hurried proceedings.
The later claims for injunction and possession relied on the earlier decree, and the lower courts treated the decree as valid without adequately examining the circumstances suggesting fraud.
issues.conclusion: The alleged family arrangement was not bona fide, and the earlier decree was fundamentally fraudulent and a nullity. The appeal was allowed, and the decrees of the courts below, including the earlier decree, were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order IV Rule 1, Order V Rule 1, Order X Rule 1 and Order XV Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a suit is commenced by plaint, summons ordinarily follows institution, and the first hearing is ordinarily when the court applies its mind to the pleadings to determine issues, not merely the returnable date of summons. The court may pronounce judgment at the first hearing if the parties are not at issue. Kanwar Singh Saini v. High Court of Delhi, together with Ved Prakash Wadhwa v. Vishwa Mohan, Sham Lal v. Atme Nand Jain Sabha, Siraj Ahmad Siddiqui v. Prem Nath Kapoor and Mangat Singh Trilochan Singh v. Satpal, explains the meaning of first hearing. A family arrangement must be bona fide, voluntary, and fair in the circumstances; it may be oral, and registration is required only when its terms are reduced to writing. The family-arrangement principles relied on include Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, Ram Charan Das v. Girija Nandini Devi, Krishna Beharilal v. Gulabchand, Maturi Pullaiah v. Maturi Narasimham and S. Shanmugam Pillai v. K. Shanmugam Pillai. A judgment obtained by fraud is a nullity and may be challenged even in collateral proceedings; fraud vitiates judicial proceedings and a court must not permit itself to be used as an instrument of fraud. The Court relied on S. B. Noronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna, S. P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath, Smt. Shrist Dhawan v. Shaw Brothers, Roshan Deen v. Preeti Lal, Ram Preeti Yadav v. U.P. Board of High School and Intermediate Education, Ram Chandra Singh v. Savitri Devi, State of Andhra Pradesh v. T. Suryachandra Rao and Hamza Haji v. State of Kerala.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_decrees_based_on_prior_consent_decree and proceedings_concluded_within_days_of_filing and defendant_was_illiterate_and_brought_on_pretext_of_other_transaction and alleged_arrangement_transferred_entire_property_without_return and no_plausible_family_dispute_or_reason_for_excluding_close_heir and defendant_retained_possession_after_decree and decree_restated_consent_without_examining_arrangement

predicates.appeal_challenges_decrees_based_on_prior: The appellant challenged later decrees that relied on an earlier decree entered after the defendant consented to the claim.
predicates.proceedings_concluded_within_days_of_fil: The plaint, admitting written statement, recorded statement, and decree followed one another within a few days.
predicates.defendant_was_illiterate_and_brought_on_: The plaintiff brought an illiterate defendant to court on the stated pretext of carrying out a different transaction.
predicates.alleged_arrangement_transferred_entire_p: The pleaded arrangement gave the defendant's entire property share to the plaintiff without any identified return to the defendant.
predicates.no_plausible_family_dispute_or_reason_fo: The plaintiff had no apparent claim or likely dispute concerning the property, and a close family member was excluded without an apparent reason.
predicates.defendant_retained_possession_after_decr: The defendant remained in possession after the decree despite the pleading that possession had been transferred to the plaintiff.
predicates.decree_restated_consent_without_examinin: The decree relied on the defendant's consent in the written statement without addressing the substance or genuineness of the alleged arrangement.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns later decrees founded on a prior consent decree and the stated circumstances show hurried proceedings, an illiterate defendant brought under a different pretext, an implausible transfer without return, continued possession, and no judicial examination of the arrangement, the prior decree is treated as a nullity for fraud.
